entities.summary:
The Purkinje effect is a phenomenon in human vision where the peak luminance sensitivity of the eye shifts toward the blue end of the color spectrum at low illumination levels. This effect was first observed by Czech physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkinje in the early 19th century, while studying the color perception of the human eye. The Purkinje effect has important implications for understanding how the human visual system adapts to low-light conditions, and has been used in a variety of applications, including photography and lighting design.

The Purkinje effect is significant because it challenges the traditional understanding of color perception and highlights the complex interactions between the human eye and the surrounding environment. By understanding the Purkinje effect, researchers can gain insights into the neural mechanisms underlying color vision and develop new technologies to improve visual perception in low-light conditions.

The Purkinje effect has far-reaching consequences for fields such as optics, photography, and lighting design. For example, it has led to the development of new types of lighting that are designed to take advantage of the Purkinje effect, such as LED lights that emit light in the blue spectrum. Additionally, the Purkinje effect has implications for our understanding of the evolution of the human visual system and the development of color vision in primates.

As Jan Purkinje himself noted, 'The blue color is the most sensitive to the eye, and the most easily perceived.' This simple yet profound comment encapsulates the significance of the Purkinje effect and its continued relevance in modern times.
